extracted.intended_audience: researchers / principal investigators preparing ERC grant applications (Starting, Consolidator, Advanced, Synergy)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and concrete heuristics for writing successful ERC proposals (B1/B2, CV/track record, and grant-level strategy) across Starting, Consolidator, Advanced and Synergy calls — focusing on demonstrating high-risk/high-gain novelty, PI independence, and credible feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part B1 (5-page Extended Synopsis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part B1 (5 pages, 'Extended Synopsis') — read by all panel reviewers; decides Step 1 evaluation (panel only); functions like NIH Specific Aims but longer. Must convey: question, ground-breaking nature, methodology, feasibility, impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat B1 as a standalone document: make the big question, the paradigm-shifting claim, and the feasibility case crystal clear for panel reviewers who will rank proposals at Step 1. Keep B1 concise yet persuasive; cover question, novelty/ground-breaking claim, high-level methods and evidence of feasibility, and expected impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Part B2 (15-page full proposal) structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Part B2 (15 pages, full proposal) — read by ad hoc external reviewers in Step 2. Typical sections: a) State of the art and objectives; b) Methodology (most pages); c) Resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use B2 to provide the technical detail that supports the bold claims in B1, especially robust methodological detail and resource justification. Expect expert external reviewers to scrutinize methods; allocate most pages to methodology and feasibility evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: B1 must work as a standalone document for Step 1
rubrics_metrics.description: B1 + CV + track record are the materials read at Step 1 by the panel; roughly ~30% of submissions pass to Step 2. B1 must work as a standalone document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure B1 alone gives panel reviewers enough to score novelty, feasibility, and PI fit — avoid referring the panel to B2 for core claims. Prioritize clarity, structure, and an explicit argument for why this deserves to pass to Step 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: CV and Track Record format and content
rubrics_metrics.description: CV and Track Record: 2 pages CV + 2 pages track record. Include 10 publications selected with rationale, narrative of major contributions, awards, invited talks, and leadership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the CV/track record to demonstrate independent excellence: select publications strategically and explain your role/contribution in each; highlight leadership, awards, invited talks and major scientific contributions that evidence PI independence and capacity to deliver the proposed project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selected publications with rationale
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide 10 publications selected with rationale, and a narrative of major contributions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't just list papers — explain why each selected output is significant and how it showcases your independence and intellectual leadership (e.g., first/last author roles, unique conceptual contributions, methods developed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground-breaking / high-risk-high-gain requirement (non-negotiable)
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC's defining criterion is high-risk/high-gain: incremental work is explicitly disfavored. Must articulate paradigm shift potential — frame: 'This will change how we think about X.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly state the transformative potential of the project; make clear how success would alter field-level understanding or capabilities. Avoid modest, incremental framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-risk/high-gain framing with feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers explicitly look for risk, BUT the proposal must demonstrate feasibility. Standard structure: bold vision + risk mitigation — 'If this works, it transforms field; if not, it still produces X, Y, Z.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pair ambitious claims with credible feasibility evidence and contingency plans. Articulate intermediate deliverables or fallback outcomes that still produce valuable science if the highest-risk elements fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-PI intellectual leadership / independence
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC funds one PI; collaborators are secondary. The PI must be the sole intellectual driver and show a track record of independent thinking. 'Senior PI parasitism' (dependence on senior mentors) is a known killer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the PI clearly the conceptual leader — demonstrate an independent research line distinct from former supervisors, and show past examples of leading work and setting research directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independence from PhD/postdoc supervisor and mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Independence from PhD/postdoc supervisor is important; career trajectory should show originality. Geographic/institutional mobility is valued; returning to home country is acceptable if scientific case is strong.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight how your project and publications diverge from former supervisors' agendas; emphasize mobility experiences and arguments showing how the host environment and career moves supported independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Starting Grant eligibility and strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting Grant specifics: 2–7 years post-PhD eligibility; junior independence narrative is critical; scope must be ambitious but feasible for an early career investigator; approximate budget ~1.5M EUR over 5 years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For Starting Grants, craft a narrative of emerging independence and show a project scope ambitious enough for ERC but feasible for an early-career PI. Use CV and track record to prove growth towards independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidator Grant eligibility and strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Consolidator Grant specifics: 7–12 years post-PhD; typically an established lab consolidating a research direction; approximate budget ~2M EUR over 5 years; track record of independent group leadership expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate group leadership, an established research direction that you will consolidate, and outputs showing you can lead and deliver a larger project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advanced Grant eligibility and strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Advanced Grant specifics: 10+ years post-PhD; requires established excellence; visionary, transformative project; approximate budget ~2.5M EUR over 5 years; track record at highest international level expected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pitch a very large, risky, and transformative research agenda rooted in a sustained record of top-level international achievement and leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synergy Grant design and justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Synergy Grants: 2–4 PIs with complementary expertise; the problem must require multiple PIs (justify why); approximate budget ~10M EUR over 6 years; specify each PI's contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify why the scientific challenge cannot be tackled by a single PI, define clear complementary roles and joint leadership, and detail governance and resource sharing among PIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 1 strategy (panel-only review and ranking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1 is panel-only: B1 + CV + track record are read by the panel; they score and rank proposals and typically ~30% pass to Step 2.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize materials for panel readers (often generalists within a panel): make claims and evidence accessible, prioritized, and compelling at the panel level; avoid relying on niche technical detail only understandable by specialists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2 strategy (external reviewers and interview preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2 involves panel + ad hoc external reviewers in the PI's exact subfield; the panel synthesizes external reviews and there may be an interview for shortlisted candidates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In B2, provide the technical depth expected by specialized external reviewers; prepare to defend novelty and feasibility in an interview and respond to likely expert critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aligning to ERC culture vs NIH expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: ERC cultural differences: ERC values single-PI vision, long-term transformative work, cross-disciplinary boundaries, European mobility narrative, and risk-taking. NIH tends to value team science, translational impact, established methodology, and productivity per dollar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the proposal language and priorities to ERC values: emphasize individual vision, transformational aims, and justified risk, rather than NIH-style team/translational framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bold vision that could change the field
rubrics_metrics.description: A bold, field-changing vision is central — proposals should convincingly explain how the work would change how we think about a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the paradigm-level claim succinctly and support it with a deliverable path; use concrete examples of potential transformative outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology with credible feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology must be sufficiently detailed and credible to convince reviewers that the high-risk aims are attainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In B2 give methodological detail, technical milestones, preliminary data or feasibility evidence, and timelines showing how the work will be carried out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk mitigation and contingency planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must build risk mitigation into the plan — risk without mitigation is penalized. Articulate fallback outputs: 'If this fails, it still produces X, Y, Z.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List specific mitigation strategies, alternative approaches, and intermediate milestones/metrics that allow progress even if the riskiest hypotheses do not hold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-disciplinary novelty (genuine interdisciplinarity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-disciplinary novelty is valued where it is genuine and necessary to the project's aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate true integration of disciplines with concrete methodological or conceptual syntheses, not just superficial or token interdisciplinarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear independence from previous mentors (anti-dependence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear evidence of independence from previous mentors is essential; a track record of dependence on senior collaborators is a liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide evidence of independent projects, distinctive contributions, independent funding or leadership roles, and a narrative that separates your intellectual trajectory from mentors'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong host institution commitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Host institution support and commitment strengthen an application (resources, environment, infrastructure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete statements or letters of support showing host commitment to facilities, space, and other resources; explain why the host environment is suitable to deliver the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: incremental project framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Incremental project framing is explicitly disfavored by ERC reviewers and will reduce competitiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid describing work as an incremental next step; instead emphasize novel hypotheses, conceptual leaps, or new methods with transformative potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: methodology too vague to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodology that is too vague to evaluate will lose — reviewers must be able to assess feasibility and approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient methodological detail and concrete workplans in B2 and sufficient evidence of feasibility in B1 so reviewers can judge the approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: over-dependence on senior collaborators
rubrics_metrics.description: A demonstrated track record of dependence on senior collaborators (senior PI parasitism) undermines claims of independence and harms the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate this by highlighting solo-led projects, first/last-author contributions, and independent leadership roles; demonstrate intellectual ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: scope too narrow for ERC ambition
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects with scope that is too narrow for ERC ambition are unlikely to win.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale the research question to match ERC expectations for high-impact, field-changing work while keeping feasibility in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: risk without mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Presenting significant risk without mitigation plans is penalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always pair risky objectives with concrete mitigation strategies and intermediate outputs to reassure reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: generic or unsupported 'impact' claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Generic 'impact' claims not supported by a credible pathway are not persuasive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make impact claims specific, plausible and linked to concrete outputs, mechanisms for uptake, or capability changes that would follow from success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: mismatch between applicant and grant level
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying to the wrong grant level (e.g., a junior investigator applying for Advanced, or vice versa) is a losing mismatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the ERC call appropriate to your career stage and evidence of independence/track record; tailor the project's ambition to that level.
